title: What are the shell's installation, startup, watcher-lifetime, SSE-reconnect and error-handling behaviours?
statement: The application is installed and run locally by the operator. Its lifecycle must be specified: how it is installed, how it starts, how long the file watcher lives relative to the server process, what a client does when the SSE stream drops, and what the operator sees when content is malformed or unreadable.
notes: ⚠️ Each of these already has a partial answer in the skeleton and none of them is written down as a contract. #73 records that `fs.watch` is unusable on Windows and chokidar is not, so the watcher choice is settled; its LIFETIME is not. The SSE reconnect behaviour matters more than it looks: a dropped stream that silently never reconnects leaves the operator reading stale state while the page looks live, which is the same class of defect as a retained workspace reported as destroyed. ⚠️ MEASURED 2026-08-27 (AST-0034, AST-0035; EVD-0055, EVD-0056, plus EVD-0051..EVD-0054 from the WHATWG specification). PROPOSAL MADE, NOT DECIDED — stage 5 is agent-proposes-user-approves. ⚠️ THE QUESTION'S OWN PREDICTION WAS RIGHT, AND UNDERSTATED. It said a silently dead stream is the same class of defect as a retained workspace reported destroyed. Measurement says the skeleton has that defect twice over and by construction: an idle stream emits ZERO bytes, so idle and dead are byte-identical, and no `id:` is ever sent, so a change during a reconnect gap is lost with nothing to recover it from. ⚠️ PROPOSAL, five parts. (1) INSTALLATION — the shell installs with the package and runs from one documented command; the detail belongs to REQ-0020 and is not settled here. (2) STARTUP — `next build` then `next start` per DEC-0018, with the watcher created as the server begins listening. (3) WATCHER LIFETIME — bound to the server process: created on listen, closed in the server's own `close()`, which the skeleton already does. ⚠️ Add what it does NOT do: there is no `watcher.on('error')` handler, so a watcher that dies takes the refresh guarantee with it and says nothing — the same defect as the stream, one layer down. (4) SSE RECONNECT — three changes, and the third is the one that removes a whole class of work. (a) A periodic comment frame, so idle and dead stop being byte-identical. (b) A client `onerror` that renders a visible disconnected state rather than leaving a live-looking page. (c) TREAT RECONNECTION ITSELF AS A CHANGE HINT and reload on it — because events are hints and never deltas (#73), a reconnecting client that reloads is exactly caught up, so `Last-Event-ID` and server-side event buffering are not needed at all. (5) ERROR HANDLING — a malformed or unreadable artifact must be visible and located, and the header must never report a count it did not render. Reporting `178` while showing 177 is worse than showing an error, because it tells the operator the missing thing is present. ⚠️ NOT MEASURED: browser reconnect behaviour (no `EventSource` in this Node build and no browser on this host — the client half is specification-only), idle timeouts beyond six seconds, concurrent clients, and malformation modes other than invalid JSON. ⚠️ NOTHING HERE TOUCHES CACHE COMPONENTS.
answer: A documented launcher owns both the application process and the watcher and terminates the watcher with the application; the binding mechanism is stage 5's to choose and validate, and nothing is claimed about `next start` today. Stream health is a NAMED heartbeat event plus a client watchdog that renders a visibly disconnected state — comment keepalives are ignored by the client parser and cannot serve. A watcher failure emits a visible signal or closes the stream; logging alone is not permitted. On reconnection the client reloads, treating reconnection as a change hint, so no event buffer or `Last-Event-ID` is needed. Malformed content is surfaced and located, and no rendered count may include an artifact the page did not render. See DEC-0022.
